title: Physics design of a dual-ring light source toward MHz-rate free-electron laser radiation
summary: Combining the high peak brilliance and short pulse duration of free-electron lasers (FELs) with the high repetition rate of diffraction-limited storage rings (DLSRs) is a promising direction for accelerator light sources. In this paper, we propose a dual-ring light source concept that, at MHz repetition rates, delivers pulses with a pulse durations and peak power intermediate between those of FELs and DLSRs. Such a light source can be realized as an upgrade of an existing DLSR by adding an isochronous ring equipped with transverse gradient undulators (TGUs) and connecting the two rings via bunch compression and decompression systems. We present the conceptual layout and show that bunch compression shortens the electron bunches to ps-scale durations; multi-turn radiation in the isochronous ring raises the repetition rate to 1.36 MHz from a single TGU; and the long TGUs enhance the brilliance, delivering $10^{7}$--$10^{9}$ photons per pulse across the soft and hard X-ray range, an increase of 2--4 orders of magnitude over the original DLSR. The dual-ring light source thus provides a cost-effective route to MHz FEL operation based on existing storage-ring infrastructure, combining the high repetition rate of a DLSR with the short pulses and high brilliance of a linac-driven FEL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dual-ring accelerator light-source concept that upgrades an existing diffraction-limited storage ring with an isochronous ring, transverse gradient undulators, and bunch compression/decompression to produce MHz-rate soft and hard X-ray pulses intermediate in duration and peak power between FELs and DLSRs.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to combine the high peak brilliance and short pulses of free-electron lasers with the high repetition rate of diffraction-limited storage rings, providing a cost-effective MHz-rate light source based on existing storage-ring infrastructure.
AI.method: The proposed layout adds an isochronous ring equipped with transverse gradient undulators to an existing DLSR and connects the rings through bunch compression and decompression systems. The paper presents the conceptual layout and assesses bunch compression, multi-turn radiation, repetition rate, and brilliance.
AI.result: Bunch compression shortens electron bunches to picosecond-scale durations; multi-turn radiation in the isochronous ring raises the repetition rate to 1.36 MHz from a single TGU; and long TGUs enhance brilliance, delivering 10^7–10^9 photons per pulse across the soft and hard X-ray range, 2–4 orders of magnitude above the original DLSR.
AI.conclusion: The dual-ring light source offers a cost-effective route to MHz FEL operation using existing storage-ring infrastructure, combining the high repetition rate of a DLSR with the short pulses and high brilliance of a linac-driven FEL.

title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 2: intensity effects and beam instabilities
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures, contribution to the CAS - CERN Accelerator School: RF for Accelerators, 18 June - 01 July 2023, Berlin, Germany
summary: In this lecture, dealing with intensity effects, the equations of longitudinal motion with induced beam voltage are analyzed. This allows us, first, to describe the single-bunch potential well distortion and the loss of Landau damping. Then the linearized Vlasov equation is used to derive step-by-step the Lebedev equation. This matrix equation is then applied to find the thresholds, growth rates and spectra of an unstable multi-bunch beam. The lecture is concluded by a discussion of possible beam-instability cures.

title: Longitudinal beam dynamics II. Lecture 1: single and double rf systems
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, contribution to the CAS - CERN Accelerator School: RF for Accelerators, 18 June - 01 July 2023, Berlin, Germany
summary: In the first part of this lecture, the main characteristics of synchrotron motion, namely, synchronous particle and phase, bucket area and emittance, are introduced. The equations of longitudinal particle motion in a single rf system of a proton synchrotron are rederived and the phase equation is analyzed for small and large amplitude particles. The particle motion below and above transition energy is also considered. The main applications and operation modes of a double rf system are discussed in the second part of the lecture. The intensity effects and beam instabilities are the subject of the following lecture.

title: Symplectic Normal Coordinates Flow for Generative Modeling of Hamiltonian Systems
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages, 6 figures plus appendices. Code: https://github.com/electronsandstuff/Normal-Coordinates-Flow
summary: In conditioned generative models of physical systems, the densities at different values of the conditioning parameters are often related through symplectic transformations. For stable linear Hamiltonian systems, there exists a symplectic transformation to "normal coordinates" such that the dynamics is reduced to rotations in each phase-space plane. This picture extends to the nonlinear case where, away from resonances, the Birkhoff normal form again consists of rotations in phase space, now with amplitude dependence. In this work, we introduce an invertible symplectic flow layer consisting of amplitude-dependent rotations in learned normal coordinates. We derive the condition under which the nonlinear rotation layer is symplectic and detail an architecture that guarantees it. Experiments are carried out on three conditional generative modeling problems: a synthetic chain of coupled nonlinear oscillators and two problems from accelerator physics. We show empirically that normalizing flows with the new layers achieve competitive or superior negative log-likelihoods compared to baseline flows, with gains that grow with the strength of the nonlinearity on the synthetic system.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an invertible symplectic flow layer based on amplitude-dependent rotations in learned normal coordinates for conditional generative modeling of Hamiltonian systems, derives and enforces the symplectic condition architecturally, and evaluates it on a synthetic nonlinear-oscillator chain and two accelerator-physics problems.
AI.motivation: Conditional generative models of physical systems often require densities at different conditioning-parameter values to be related by symplectic transformations. Normal-coordinate and Birkhoff-normal-form theory reduce linear and, away from resonances, nonlinear Hamiltonian dynamics to phase-space rotations, motivating flow layers that exploit this structure.
AI.method: The authors construct a symplectic flow layer consisting of amplitude-dependent rotations in learned normal coordinates. They derive the condition under which the nonlinear rotation layer is symplectic and specify an architecture that guarantees it, then incorporate these layers into normalizing flows for conditional generative modeling.
AI.result: Experiments address a synthetic chain of coupled nonlinear oscillators and two accelerator-physics problems. Normalizing flows with the new layers achieve competitive or superior negative log-likelihoods relative to baseline flows, and on the synthetic system the gains increase with nonlinearity strength.
AI.conclusion: The proposed normal-coordinate symplectic flow provides an effective structure-preserving inductive bias for conditional generative modeling of Hamiltonian systems, with particular benefit under stronger nonlinearity in the synthetic test. The abstract does not provide quantitative values or broader benchmarking details.

title: Status of Accelerator Automation in the Community: Classification, Survey Results, and the Role of AI and Machine Learning
comment: 4 pages, 5 figures. Contribution to IPAC'26, Deauville, France, 17-22 May 2026, paper WEP6099
summary: The increasing complexity of particle accelerators and the growing demand for operational efficiency have intensified the focus on automation in accelerator control systems. However, there is still a lack of a common language to describe and compare the level of automation across different facilities. This article presents a generic classification scheme for accelerator automation, defining five distinct levels ranging from basic operational assistance to full autonomy. To assess the current state of automation in the accelerator community, a structured survey was conducted during the 14th Workshop on Accelerator Operations (WAO 2025). Responses from major laboratories indicate that more than one third of accelerators currently operate at the lowest level 1 (operational assistance), and no facility has yet reached full automation. However, projections show a clear trend toward higher levels within the next decade. Key drivers include optimization algorithms for autotuning, finite-state machines, and closed-loop feedback systems. This study provides both a conceptual framework and a snapshot of current implementation practices, supporting a shared understanding of accelerator automation across the community.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a five-level classification scheme for particle accelerator automation and reports a WAO 2025 survey showing that more than one third of responding accelerators operate at the lowest level, none are fully autonomous, and higher automation levels are projected within the next decade.
AI.motivation: Particle accelerators are becoming more complex and require greater operational efficiency, but the accelerator community lacks a common language for describing and comparing automation levels across facilities.
AI.method: The authors define a generic five-level accelerator automation classification ranging from basic operational assistance to full autonomy, then conduct a structured community survey during the 14th Workshop on Accelerator Operations (WAO 2025), collecting responses from major laboratories.
AI.result: Survey responses indicate that more than one third of accelerators currently operate at level 1, operational assistance, and no facility has reached full automation. title: Optimizing an RFSoC LLRF Controller for a Low-PRF, Short Pulse System
summary: The Advanced Light Source (ALS) LINAC operates with 3 GHz RF pulses at 0.7 Hz pulse repetition frequency (PRF) and 1.2 microsecond duration, imposing severe limitations on traditional PID and adaptive feedforward control schemes. An RFSoC-based controller prototype was developed and presented in prior work to upgrade the legacy LLRF systems for the LINAC and Subharmonic Buncher. This paper presents sampling scheme optimizations and interleaving calibration techniques for RFSoC based control of pulsed RF systems. We detail bench characterization methodologies to isolate component-level phase noise across individual ADC, DAC, and clock components in the Xilinx ZCU208 hardware ecosystem. Finally, we explore translating open-loop controller bench measurements into controller-added closed-loop LLRF performance predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper reports sampling-scheme optimizations and interleaving calibration techniques for an RFSoC-based low-level RF (LLRF) controller intended for the ALS LINAC's 3 GHz, 1.2 µs RF pulses at 0.7 Hz PRF, together with bench methods for isolating component-level phase noise in the Xilinx ZCU208 ecosystem and an approach for predicting closed-loop LLRF performance from open-loop bench measurements.
AI.motivation: The ALS LINAC's 3 GHz pulses have 0.7 Hz PRF and 1.2 µs duration, which severely limits conventional PID and adaptive feedforward control schemes; an RFSoC-based controller prototype was previously developed to upgrade the legacy LLRF systems for the LINAC and Subharmonic Buncher, and its sampling and calibration performance now needs optimization.

title: Physics in Safety and Safety in Physics: Lessons from the LHC and its Underground Experiments
summary: Large underground particle-physics facilities are usually discussed by separating scientific performance from the systems that make their operation safe. We develop a complementary view in which safety is treated as an intrinsic part of the physical and operational structure of an experiment. Using the LHC, ATLAS, and CMS as principal case studies, we introduce the concepts of physics in safety and safety in physics: physical laws, measurements, and models determine hazards and protective barriers, while those barriers in turn define the machine, detector, access, and intervention states in which physics can be performed. We formulate this relation through a \emph{safe operational phase space} and through admissible trajectories connecting different configurations, emphasizing that safety constrains not only states but also transitions between them. The framework is applied to beam and magnet protection, cryogenic and oxygen-deficiency hazards, detector-specific risk configurations, personnel access, maintenance, and radiation protection, with particular attention to the different architectures of ATLAS and CMS. We argue that validated protection does not merely restrict scientific activity but can enlarge the domain of sustainable operation. This viewpoint provides a unified physical and operational framework for understanding safety at the LHC and for incorporating protection, maintainability, and recoverability into the design of future accelerator and underground facilities such as HL-LHC, FCC and muon collider.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified framework treating safety as intrinsic to the physical and operational structure of underground particle-physics experiments, using the LHC, ATLAS, and CMS to show how protection systems constrain and enable feasible operation.
AI.motivation: Conventional discussions of large underground particle-physics facilities separate scientific performance from operational safety. The paper argues for a complementary view in which safety is an intrinsic part of an experiment’s physical and operational structure.
AI.method: Using the LHC, ATLAS, and CMS as principal case studies, the authors introduce “physics in safety” and “safety in physics,” formulate the relationship through a safe operational phase space and admissible trajectories between configurations, and apply the framework to beam and magnet protection, cryogenic and oxygen-deficiency hazards, detector-specific risks, personnel access, maintenance, and radiation protection.
AI.result: The framework shows that safety constrains not only permissible states but also transitions between them, and that validated protection can enlarge the domain of sustainable operation rather than merely restrict scientific activity. The paper also highlights differences between the ATLAS and CMS architectures.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that this viewpoint provides a unified physical and operational framework for understanding safety at the LHC and for incorporating protection, maintainability, and recoverability into the design of future accelerator and underground facilities such as HL-LHC, FCC, and a muon collider.

title: Beam-beam effects on measurements at electron-positron colliders: LEP neutrino counting and Higgs factories
comment: 40 pages, 14 figures, 18 tables, pre-print for reference at LCWS2026
summary: Beam-beam electromagnetic interactions affect the luminosity, collision energy, polarization, and particle backgrounds relevant to precision measurements at electron-positron colliders. We investigate these effects using Fast $e^{\pm}e^{\pm}$ Beam and Luminosity (FeeBL), a new beam-beam simulation framework, and compare its predictions with published results from LEP and proposed future colliders. We reproduce the analytical field-integration calculations of LEP Bhabha scattering and identify an approximately 2% bias in previously published beam-deflection simulations. Applying the corresponding luminosity correction and a revised uncertainty assessment motivated by the observed agreement among the four LEP experiments yields ($N_ν= 2.9965 \pm 0.0040$), compared with the previously reported ($2.9963 \pm 0.0074$). The revised uncertainty is conditional on an assumed common rescaling of experiment specific uncertainties and motivates further investigation of the original uncertainty budgets. We identify and correct implementation errors in the modeling of Breit-Wheeler, Bethe-Heitler, and Landau-Lifshitz pair production, with implications for detector backgrounds at Higgs factories. Simulated beam depolarization and luminosity spectra are compared with existing ILC and HALHF predictions. Finally, we investigate collision energy monochromatization for direct Higgs production, obtaining sub-MeV collision energy peak widths in exploratory linear collider configurations at substantial luminosity cost, while finding significantly weaker narrowing for the FCC-ee configurations studied. We derive a rigid Gaussian beam overlap model and estimate that FCC-ee needs roughly 10 m of horizontal only dispersion to reach widths of $\approx1~\mathrm{MeV}$.

The work aims to validate a new simulation framework against published LEP and future-collider results and to quantify implications for neutrino counting, detector backgrounds at Higgs factories, and monochromatization.

They reproduce analytical field-integration calculations of LEP Bhabha scattering, quantify a bias in prior beam-deflection simulations, apply a luminosity correction and revised uncertainty assessment, correct implementation errors in Breit-Wheeler, Bethe-Heitler, and Landau-Lifshitz pair production, compare simulated beam depolarization and luminosity spectra with ILC and HALHF predictions, and investigate collision-energy monochromatization, including a derived rigid Gaussian beam overlap model.
AI.result: The authors identify an approximately 2% bias in previously published beam-deflection simulations and obtain Nν = 2.9965 ± 0.0040 after the corresponding luminosity correction and revised uncertainty assessment, compared with the previously reported 2.9963 ± 0.0074; the revised uncertainty is conditional on an assumed common rescaling of experiment-specific uncertainties. They also correct pair-production implementation errors with implications for detector backgrounds at Higgs factories, compare depolarization and luminosity spectra with ILC and HALHF predictions, obtain sub-MeV collision-energy peak widths in exploratory linear-collider configurations at substantial luminosity cost but significantly weaker narrowing for the studied FCC-ee configurations, and estimate that FCC-ee needs roughly 10 m of horizontal-only dispersion to reach widths of about 1 MeV.

title: Effects of pulse durations in atom interferometry with double Raman diffraction
summary: Double Raman diffraction is a key enabling technique for future space missions relying on atom interferometry that offers enhanced sensitivity and intrinsic suppression of systematic effects. This diffraction mechanism naturally arises when employing a retro-reflection configuration in microgravity, but then accelerations can no longer be determined through a frequency-chirp scan. As a consequence, measurements become much more sensitive to systematic effects associated with pulse timing and duration. Indeed, the finite pulse duration can introduce additional phase shifts and small modifications of the arm trajectories, which are critical sources of error in high-precision measurements. In this work, we present the first complete analytical results of these effects for double Raman diffraction, building upon previous work for single diffraction and extending the standard literature. Our analysis determines the impact of finite pulse durations on the full interferometer sequence, quantifying the shifts of the atomic wave packets' trajectories and the acquired phases. The description relies on a comprehensive framework describing matter-wave propagation in terms of central trajectories and centered wave packets, and can be easily incorporated into relativistic treatments. Furthermore, we make use of group theoretic methods that are particularly useful when accounting for residual accelerations and frequency chirps, which are also relevant for ground-based applications. Our study includes time-dependent accelerations and frequency chirps, gravity gradients, retardation effects, AC Stark shifts induced by the Raman pulses, and external forces such those due to magnetic fields or temperature gradients in the black-body radiation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a first complete analytical treatment of finite-pulse-duration effects in atom interferometry using double Raman diffraction, quantifying wave-packet trajectory shifts and phase shifts across the full interferometer sequence.
AI.motivation: Double Raman diffraction is important for future space-based atom interferometry because it provides high sensitivity and intrinsic suppression of systematic effects. In microgravity retro-reflection configurations, accelerations cannot be measured by a frequency-chirp scan, making measurements more sensitive to pulse-timing and pulse-duration systematics. Finite pulse durations can produce additional phase shifts and alter arm trajectories, which are critical errors in high-precision measurements.
AI.method: The authors develop analytical results for double Raman diffraction, extending prior work on single diffraction and standard treatments. They describe matter-wave propagation using central trajectories and centered wave packets, apply group-theoretic methods for residual accelerations and frequency chirps, and analyze the full interferometer sequence including time-dependent accelerations and chirps, gravity gradients, retardation effects, AC Stark shifts from Raman pulses, and external forces such as magnetic-field or black-body-radiation temperature-gradient effects.
AI.result: The analysis determines how finite pulse durations affect the complete interferometer sequence, quantifying shifts of atomic wave-packet trajectories and acquired phases. The framework is suitable for incorporation into relativistic treatments and for group-theoretic accounting of residual accelerations and frequency chirps. No experimental sensitivity or numerical performance results are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Finite pulse durations introduce trajectory and phase corrections that must be accounted for in high-precision double Raman atom interferometry, including space and ground-based applications. The presented analytical framework extends standard literature and can support relativistic and systematic-effect analyses.

title: HFR distorted-wave photoionization of Te III: a preliminary benchmark for large-scale atomic data production to model nebular-phase kilonovae
summary: The shortage of photoionization cross sections for heavy elements remains an obstacle to non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) modeling of nebular-phase kilonova ejecta, where hydrogenic prescriptions have often been adopted in the absence of ion-specific calculations. We present a first preliminary benchmark of direct photoionization cross sections for doubly ionized tellurium, obtained using the distorted-wave (DW) approximation within the pseudo-relativistic Hartree-Fock (HFR) method implemented in the Cowan codes, in which a semi-empirical adjustment based on the observed energy levels is performed. For the photoionization from the ground level of Te III to the ground level of Te IV, comparison with Dirac R-matrix data shows encouraging agreement in the magnitude and overall decrease of the non-resonant background in the lower photon-energy region, approximately below 4 Ry (autoionizing resonances are absent from the present direct treatment). These preliminary results support HFR distorted-wave calculations as a promising and computationally tractable approach for large-scale production of photoionization cross sections, with lanthanides and actinides as longer-term targets, in light of their importance to kilonova modeling and of the severe lack of atomic data for these species.

AI.tldr: A preliminary HFR distorted-wave calculation produces direct photoionization cross sections for Te III, showing encouraging agreement with Dirac R-matrix data below about 4 Ry and supporting large-scale atomic data production for nebular-phase kilonova modeling.
AI.motivation: Heavy-element photoionization cross sections are scarce, hindering NLTE modeling of nebular-phase kilonova ejecta; hydrogenic prescriptions have often been used because ion-specific calculations are unavailable.
AI.method: Direct photoionization cross sections for doubly ionized tellurium were calculated with the distorted-wave approximation in the pseudo-relativistic Hartree-Fock method using the Cowan codes, including a semi-empirical adjustment based on observed energy levels. Autoionizing resonances were not included.
AI.result: For photoionization from the Te III ground level to the Te IV ground level, the non-resonant background magnitude and its overall decrease at lower photon energies, approximately below 4 Ry, show encouraging agreement with Dirac R-matrix data.
AI.conclusion: The preliminary results support HFR distorted-wave calculations as a promising and computationally tractable route to large-scale photoionization cross-section production, with lanthanides and actinides as longer-term targets for kilonova modeling.

title: Rapid high-purity loading of barium ion via relayed selectivity from naturally abundant source
comment: 16 pages, 4 main-text figures and 7 supplemental figures, including Supplemental Material
summary: Trapped ions is one of the promising platforms for realizing quantum information processing and quantum simulation. Selective and rapid loading of a specific isotope lays the critical foundation for such purpose particularly when scaling up the system size. Here we demonstrate a new method for rapid isotope-selective loading of $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ or $^{135}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$, two types of promising ion qubits, from naturally abundant source using a three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme. Neutral atoms are selected on the narrow 791 nm $6s^2\,{}^1S_0\rightarrow6s6p\,{}^3P_1^o$ transition, resonantly transferred at 554 nm to $6s6d\,{}^3D_1$, and ionized using an existing 532 nm Raman beam. A spectral-overlap analysis based on isotope and hyperfine shifts shows relayed selectivity that the second step can further suppress undesired-isotope excitation and no contaminant ion is detected during our entire experiment. Besides, the resonant drive of the second step excitation yields a prominent loading rate of the selected species. This strategy using multi-step excitations to establish relayed selectivity can be extended to high-purity loading of other species of ions.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates rapid, high-purity isotope-selective loading of 137Ba+ or 135Ba+ from a naturally abundant source using a three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme with relayed selectivity.
AI.motivation: Trapped ions are promising platforms for quantum information processing and quantum simulation, and scaling these systems requires selective, rapid loading of specific isotopes with minimal contaminants.
AI.method: Neutral barium atoms are selected on the narrow 791 nm 6s^2 1S0→6s6p 3P1o transition, resonantly transferred at 554 nm to 6s6d 3D1, and ionized by an existing 532 nm Raman beam. A spectral-overlap analysis based on isotope and hyperfine shifts establishes relayed selectivity, with the second step further suppressing excitation of undesired isotopes.
AI.result: The scheme achieves rapid isotope-selective loading of 137Ba+ or 135Ba+ from a naturally abundant source, yields a prominent loading rate for the selected species, and shows no contaminant ions detected throughout the experiment.
AI.conclusion: Multi-step excitation can provide relayed selectivity for high-purity loading of barium ion isotopes and may be extended to other ion species.

title: Consistent Mapping for Fluid Structure Interaction with Geometrically Nonlinear Isogeometric Beams
summary: Isogeometric beam formulations provide an efficient reduced-dimensional representation of slender structures, combining accurate geometry and high-order continuity with few structural degrees of freedom. Their application to fluid--structure interaction (FSI) requires transferring motion and loads between the one-dimensional beam centerline and the surrounding fluid interface. While mapping strategies exist for conventional finite element beams, geometrically nonlinear isogeometric formulations require operators consistent with their spline-based kinematics and distinct descriptions of cross-sectional rotation. This work develops consistent beam-to-surface mappings for geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams in partitioned FSI. Fluid-interface points are attached to the beam in the reference configuration and reconstructed using the nonlinear kinematics of each formulation. Consistent linearization yields a configuration-dependent mapping operator whose transpose ensures work-conjugate load transfer. The formulations are verified through analytical deformation tests, convergence studies, and virtual-work checks, and evaluated in beam-based adaptations of the Mok and Turek--Hron benchmarks and the Goland wing flutter benchmark. The results confirm accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations, while demonstrating the applicability of both beam formulations to coupled FSI problems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops consistent beam-to-surface mapping operators for geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams in partitioned fluid–structure interaction, enabling accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations, with verification and benchmark evaluations.
AI.motivation: Isogeometric beam formulations offer efficient reduced-dimensional modeling of slender structures, but their use in fluid–structure interaction requires transferring motion and loads between the one-dimensional beam centerline and the surrounding fluid interface. Existing mapping strategies for conventional finite element beams are not consistent with the spline-based kinematics and distinct cross-sectional rotation descriptions of geometrically nonlinear isogeometric beam formulations.
AI.method: Fluid-interface points are attached to the beam in the reference configuration and reconstructed using the nonlinear kinematics of each geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli or Timoshenko beam formulation. Consistent linearization yields a configuration-dependent mapping operator, whose transpose ensures work-conjugate load transfer. The formulations are verified using analytical deformation tests, convergence studies, and virtual-work checks, and evaluated in beam-based adaptations of the Mok and Turek–Hron benchmarks and the Goland wing flutter benchmark.
AI.result: The results confirm accurate interface reconstruction and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations. Both geometrically nonlinear isogeometric beam formulations are shown to be applicable to coupled fluid–structure interaction problems in the considered verification and benchmark cases.
AI.conclusion: Consistent beam-to-surface mappings enable partitioned fluid–structure interaction with geometrically nonlinear isogeometric Bernoulli and Timoshenko beams, providing accurate interface kinematics and work-conjugate load transfer under large deformations. The abstract does not provide quantitative error or performance values.

title: High-sensitivity sensing technology of 10 MHz radio frequency electric field based on Rydberg atoms
summary: To address the pressing need for high-sensitivity, miniaturized electric field sensors in the short-wave communication band (3-30 MHz), this study proposes and demonstrates a radio frequency electric field quantum sensing scheme based on cesium atomic Rydberg states and the electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) effect. The scheme employs an all-infrared optical design, utilizing 852 nm probe light, 1470 nm dressing light, and 780 nm coupling light to efficiently prepare the 49P3/2 Rydberg state in a room-temperature cesium vapor cell, which is then probed non-destructively via ladder-type four-level EIT spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and demonstrates an all-infrared Rydberg-atom quantum sensing scheme for 10 MHz radio-frequency electric fields, using ladder-type four-level electromagnetically induced transparency in a room-temperature cesium vapor cell; quantitative performance is not reported in the abstract.
AI.motivation: There is a pressing need for high-sensitivity, miniaturized electric field sensors in the short-wave communication band from 3 to 30 MHz.
AI.method: The scheme uses cesium atomic Rydberg states and the electromagnetically induced transparency effect. An all-infrared optical design employs 852 nm probe light, 1470 nm dressing light, and 780 nm coupling light to prepare the 49P3/2 Rydberg state in a room-temperature cesium vapor cell, which is probed non-destructively by ladder-type four-level EIT spectroscopy.

title: Efficient sensitivity analysis for combustion problems via reformulation and adjoint methods
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables; Supplementary Material (9 pages) included
summary: Numerical simulations of combustion processes rely on chemical kinetic models, whose predictive capability is typically assessed by comparing measurements of quantities of interest (QoIs) in idealized experimental configurations with the corresponding simulated values. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the influence of model parameters on QoIs, making it a key tool for model development and optimization. Given the large number of parameters involved in detailed kinetic models compared to the number of QoIs, adjoint methods are a promising approach for efficient sensitivity analysis. Ignition delay times (IDTs) and extinction strain rates (ESRs) are among the QoIs of primary importance. However, applying adjoint methods to these quantities is not straightforward and is addressed in this work. The system of governing equations is reformulated via a coordinate transformation that makes the QoI an explicit component of the solution vector. This reformulation enables the application of adjoint sensitivity analysis for both IDT and ESR. A computational complexity analysis demonstrates that the proposed formulation significantly improves algorithmic efficiency compared to conventional approaches. The methodology is verified by comparing adjoint sensitivity coefficients with those obtained from other methods. Execution time measurements show computational cost reductions of up to two orders of magnitude relative to standard direct sensitivity analysis. A benchmark study is conducted across kinetic models of increasing size to assess how far theoretical efficiency gains are realized in practice. While the results show that implementation details can limit performance for smaller problem sizes, the expected asymptotic scaling is observed for larger models. The benchmark thus provides a reference framework for identifying key performance bottlenecks and guiding subsequent optimization efforts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a reformulation that enables adjoint sensitivity analysis for ignition delay times and extinction strain rates in combustion kinetic models, verifies it against other methods, and benchmarks computational efficiency across models of increasing size.
AI.motivation: Detailed chemical kinetic models contain many parameters, while combustion simulations typically provide relatively few quantities of interest. Adjoint methods are therefore attractive for efficient sensitivity analysis, but applying them to ignition delay times and extinction strain rates is not straightforward.
AI.method: The governing equations are reformulated through a coordinate transformation that makes the quantity of interest an explicit component of the solution vector. This allows adjoint sensitivity analysis to be applied to both ignition delay times and extinction strain rates. The methodology is verified by comparing adjoint sensitivity coefficients with those from other methods, supported by computational complexity analysis and execution-time measurements.

title: Offline Evaluation of Information-Theoretic Adaptive Bayesian Vector Magnetometry
summary: An information-theoretic adaptive Bayesian framework for jointly estimating the longitudinal and transverse components of a magnetic field from the time-resolved optical response of a cold $^{87}$Rb ensemble is presented. A linearly polarized continuous-wave probe drives the $D_2$ $F{=}1 \rightarrow F'{=}0$ transition, producing coherent population trapping (CPT) lineshapes whose width, contrast, and transient dynamics depend sensitively on the ambient magnetic field. The full temporal signal, including early-time transient signal and the steady-state absorption, is compared against a precomputed Maxwell-Bloch forward model. The joint posterior distributions of the longitudinal and transverse components of the magnetic field are updated sequentially, while marginalizing over instrumental nuisance parameters arising from the finite resolution of the magnetic bias coil supply. At each step, the applied longitudinal bias field is chosen to maximize the expected Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the current prior and the anticipated posterior, the expected information gain. As a proof of principle, the protocol is validated in post-processing on pre-recorded experimental scans, and both field components converge to well localized field estimates with weak correlation between them, consistent with the distinct dependence of the CPT resonance position and lineshape on the field components. These results establish an information-theoretic framework for joint vector field estimation from transient cold-atom spectroscopy. However, there exists a systematic forward-model discrepancy, showing that posterior concentration alone does not establish accuracy and motivating nuisance-parameter inference in future online implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents and offline-validates an information-theoretic adaptive Bayesian protocol that jointly estimates longitudinal and transverse magnetic-field components from the time-resolved optical response of a cold 87Rb ensemble, using coherent population trapping lineshapes and a Maxwell-Bloch forward model, while identifying a systematic forward-model discrepancy.
AI.motivation: The work aims to enable joint vector magnetic-field estimation from transient cold-atom spectroscopy and to select applied bias fields that maximize expected information gain, while accounting for instrumental nuisance parameters.
AI.method: A linearly polarized continuous-wave probe drives the D2 F=1 to F'=0 transition in a cold 87Rb ensemble, producing coherent population trapping lineshapes. The full temporal signal, including early-time transients and steady-state absorption, is compared with a precomputed Maxwell-Bloch forward model. Joint posteriors for the longitudinal and transverse field components are updated sequentially while marginalizing over nuisance parameters from finite magnetic bias-coil resolution; at each step, the longitudinal bias field is chosen to maximize the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence between prior and anticipated posterior. The protocol is validated in post-processing on pre-recorded experimental scans.

A systematic forward-model discrepancy is also observed, showing that posterior concentration alone does not establish accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The results establish an information-theoretic framework for joint vector field estimation from transient cold-atom spectroscopy. The forward-model discrepancy motivates nuisance-parameter inference in future online implementations.

title: GPU acceleration of the numerical-atomic-orbital DFT code OpenMX with GEMMul8: performance and numerical agreement on consumer and HPC GPUs
summary: We integrate GEMMul8, a library that emulates FP64 matrix multiplication on INT8 Tensor Cores, into the GPU version of the numerical-atomic-orbital first-principles code OpenMX 4.0. The GEMMul8 configuration is compared against the cuBLAS FP64 configuration within each of two environments, a consumer GeForce RTX 5080 and an HPC-oriented H100 PCIe, for the four computational paths formed by collinear (CL) or noncollinear (NCL) spin and band or $Γ$-point-cluster solvers. In fixed-work measurements that completed 25 SCF iterations, the diagonalization section of a 384-atom CL band calculation on the RTX 5080 is accelerated by a factor of 2.1 and the total run time by 1.8; a 512-atom CL cluster calculation, which uses only real matrix products in contrast to the CL band calculation, still gains a factor of 1.5 in the diagonalization section. On the H100, GEMMul8 provides little additional acceleration of the diagonalization section. In an accuracy test on a 216-atom Si system in which one atom was displaced by 0.05 angstrom, all 24 configurations were converged using an SCF convergence criterion of $10^{-8}$; every configuration converged at the same iteration within each path, and the differences between GEMMul8 and cuBLAS are at most $2\times10^{-12}$ Ha in the total energy and $7\times10^{-12}$ Ha/Bohr in force components.

AI.tldr: GEMMul8, which emulates FP64 matrix multiplication on INT8 Tensor Cores, was integrated into the GPU version of OpenMX 4.0 and compared with cuBLAS FP64 on an RTX 5080 and an H100 PCIe. It accelerated diagonalization and total runtime on the consumer GPU, gave little additional acceleration on the H100, and preserved numerical agreement within tight tolerances.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether GEMMul8-based FP64 emulation on INT8 Tensor Cores can accelerate the GPU version of OpenMX across consumer and HPC GPU environments while maintaining numerical agreement with cuBLAS FP64.
AI.method: GEMMul8 was integrated into GPU OpenMX 4.0 and compared with cuBLAS FP64 on a GeForce RTX 5080 and an H100 PCIe for four computational paths combining collinear or noncollinear spin with band or Γ-point-cluster solvers. Fixed-work tests used 25 SCF iterations, and accuracy was tested on a 216-atom Si system with one atom displaced by 0.05 angstrom using an SCF convergence criterion of 10^-8.
AI.result: On the RTX 5080, a 384-atom CL band calculation achieved 2.1× acceleration in the diagonalization section and 1.8× in total runtime; a 512-atom CL cluster calculation gained 1.5× in diagonalization. On the H100, GEMMul8 provided little additional diagonalization acceleration. All 24 accuracy configurations converged, at the same iteration within each path, with maximum differences of 2×10^-12 Ha in total energy and 7×10^-12 Ha/Bohr in force components versus cuBLAS.
AI.conclusion: GEMMul8 provides worthwhile acceleration for the tested OpenMX workloads on the consumer RTX 5080 but little additional benefit on the H100 PCIe, while maintaining numerical agreement with cuBLAS FP64 within the reported tolerances.

title: A versatile beamline for attosecond photoelectron and photon spectroscopy
summary: We report on the development of a versatile attosecond beamline for ultrafast spectroscopy of atoms and molecules, as well as for the metrology of infrared laser pulses. Using a few-cycle pulse (approximately 5 fs) for driving the high-order harmonic generation process, we show that the modulation of the harmonic flux in the cut-off spectral region, induced by a weak perturbing field, enables complete electric-field characterization of the perturbing pulse. Phase-sensitive detection with a lock-in amplifier further reveals polarization-dependent effects, observed as modulations at twice the fundamental optical frequency, emphasizing the sub-laser-cycle electronic control inherent to the measurement technique. In addition, the beamline supports the implementation of two-color (extreme ultraviolet and infrared) phase-sensitive experiments using approximately 30 fs pulses and a velocity map imaging spectrometer (VMI). This configuration will enable the study of photoemission time delays in atomic and molecular systems. Together, these results establish the beamline as a robust and adaptable platform for probing attosecond dynamics across diverse experimental approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a versatile attosecond beamline for ultrafast spectroscopy of atoms and molecules and for infrared laser-pulse metrology. Using few-cycle-driven high-order harmonic generation, it demonstrates electric-field characterization from harmonic-flux modulation and supports two-color XUV/IR phase-sensitive photoelectron experiments.
AI.motivation: To establish a robust, adaptable platform for probing attosecond dynamics in atomic and molecular systems and for characterizing infrared laser fields, spanning photoelectron/photon spectroscopy and laser-pulse metrology.
AI.method: A few-cycle pulse of approximately 5 fs drives high-order harmonic generation. A weak perturbing field modulates the harmonic flux in the cutoff spectral region, enabling reconstruction of the perturbing pulse electric field. Phase-sensitive lock-in detection resolves polarization-dependent modulations at twice the fundamental optical frequency. The beamline also combines approximately 30 fs extreme-ultraviolet and infrared pulses with a velocity map imaging spectrometer for two-color phase-sensitive experiments.
AI.result: The beamline enables complete electric-field characterization of the perturbing pulse and reveals polarization-dependent harmonic-flux modulations at twice the fundamental optical frequency, indicating sub-laser-cycle electronic control. It is also configured for XUV/IR photoemission time-delay studies; specific time-delay measurements or quantitative performance metrics are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The beamline is a robust and adaptable platform for attosecond spectroscopy and laser-field metrology, supporting both few-cycle high-order-harmonic-generation-based field characterization and two-color XUV/IR photoelectron experiments.

title: Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions for the Spectral Difference method on simplex elements
summary: Unsteady compressible simulations with high-order methods on unstructured meshes require boundaries that let acoustic, entropy and vorticity waves leave the domain without spurious reflection. For the spectral difference (SD) method, the Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions (NSCBC) have only been formulated on quadrilaterals and hexahedra. Their strong-form formalism relies on a line of flux points normal to the boundary face, which does not exist on triangles and tetrahedra. This paper extends the NSCBC to the SD method on simplex elements, including multi-species reacting gases. The characteristic analysis is performed in the physical frame of each flux point of the boundary face, and the normal derivative of the normal flux is evaluated using the Raviart-Thomas divergence operator. The boundary fluxes are recovered from a linear system local to each boundary element, whose matrix depends on the geometry only. The treatment is compared with the tensor-product formulation at a comparable number of degrees of freedom on a series of test cases covering acoustic, vortical, viscous and reacting flows on triangles and tetrahedra. In all cases, the results are in close agreement with those obtained on quadrilaterals and hexahedra, so that the NSCBC become available for the SD method on simplex meshes, which are well suited to complex geometries.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions (NSCBC) to the spectral difference method on triangular and tetrahedral meshes, including multi-species reacting gases, and validates the formulation against tensor-product quadrilateral/hexahedral results on acoustic, vortical, viscous, and reacting test cases.
AI.motivation: Unsteady compressible high-order simulations on unstructured meshes require nonreflecting boundaries for acoustic, entropy, and vorticity waves. NSCBC for the spectral difference method had only been formulated on quadrilaterals and hexahedra because their strong-form treatment relies on a line of flux points normal to the boundary face, which is unavailable on simplex elements.
AI.method: The NSCBC are extended to spectral difference discretizations on simplex elements. Characteristic analysis is performed in the physical frame of each flux point on the boundary face, and the normal derivative of the normal flux is evaluated with the Raviart-Thomas divergence operator. Boundary fluxes are recovered from a linear system local to each boundary element, with a matrix depending only on geometry. The formulation includes multi-species reacting gases and is tested on triangles and tetrahedra.
AI.result: Across test cases covering acoustic, vortical, viscous, and reacting flows on triangles and tetrahedra, the proposed treatment agrees closely with the tensor-product formulation at a comparable number of degrees of freedom on quadrilaterals and hexahedra.
AI.conclusion: NSCBC are now available for the spectral difference method on simplex meshes, which are well suited to complex geometries.

title: Dynamics of singular-jet formation during the collapse of drop-impact craters
summary: The collapse of a drop-impact crater that bypasses the pinch-off singularity produces exceptionally thin, high-velocity jets, often referred to as singular-jets. We perform 2D axisymmetric DNS using Basilisk, employing adaptive mesh refinement to capture the intricate flow features. The numerical results for a drop diameter of $3.64$ mm at ambient pressure match the experiments well under different impact conditions. During the crater collapse, qualitatively different dimple shapes form, including an entrapped bubble beneath the dimple. Quantitatively, an entrapped bubble with a diameter of ~210 μm and a jet velocity of 61.7 m/s for the singular-jet case during cylindrical dimple collapse is obtained from simulations. Subtle morphological changes in crater evolution distinguish the jetting regime, with a critical angle of 109.2 between the crater side wall and its base in the singular-jet case. The simulation provides insight into the internal flow fields, enabling us to delineate the observed phenomenon. The pressure and velocity fields reveal that the high jetting velocity is associated with the formation and rapid collapse of a nearly cylindrical dimple. The resulting pressure distribution drives a strongly upward flow near the dimple base, while the nearly parallel dimple side walls redirect radial liquid motion towards the axis. We extend the simulations into the post-entrainment region and identify another singular-jet near the upper boundary of the entrainment region. The jet reaches a velocity of 63.93 m/s and exhibits morphological characteristics similar to the first singular-jet case. A regime map is constructed from simulations spanning Weber numbers ranging from 100 to 200 and Froude numbers from 45 to 92; the updated lower and upper boundaries for the entrainment region, based on singular-jet formation, are We = 45.5\, Fr^{0.237} and We = 53.5\, Fr^{0.251}, respectively.

AI.tldr: Two-dimensional axisymmetric direct numerical simulations with adaptive mesh refinement reproduce drop-impact crater collapse and reveal the flow mechanisms, dimple morphologies, and regime boundaries governing singular-jet formation.
AI.motivation: The collapse of a drop-impact crater that bypasses pinch-off produces exceptionally thin, high-velocity singular jets, motivating a detailed numerical study of the internal flow, crater morphology, and conditions that distinguish jetting from non-jetting regimes.
AI.method: The authors perform 2D axisymmetric direct numerical simulations using Basilisk with adaptive mesh refinement for a 3.64 mm drop at ambient pressure under different impact conditions. They analyze pressure and velocity fields, extend simulations into the post-entrainment region, and construct a regime map from simulations with Weber numbers from 100 to 200 and Froude numbers from 45 to 92.
AI.result: Simulations match experiments under different impact conditions. Singular-jet cases show qualitatively different dimple shapes, including an entrapped bubble about 210 μm in diameter and a jet velocity of 61.7 m/s during cylindrical dimple collapse, with a critical crater side-wall-to-base angle of 109.2 degrees. A post-entrainment singular jet reaches 63.93 m/s and resembles the first jet. Updated entrainment-region boundaries based on singular-jet formation are We = 45.5 Fr^0.237 and We = 53.5 Fr^0.251.
AI.conclusion: High jetting velocity is associated with formation and rapid collapse of a nearly cylindrical dimple. The resulting pressure distribution drives strongly upward flow near the dimple base, while nearly parallel side walls redirect radial liquid motion toward the axis. The study also identifies a second singular jet in the post-entrainment region and provides updated Weber-Froude regime boundaries for singular-jet formation.

title: On the Method of Projection onto Localized States for Describing Reactions and Clustering
summary: The method of projection onto localized states intended for describing reactions and clustering is examined. In particular, the method offers a simple extension of the no-core shell model to continuum- and clusterized bound states. A critical analysis of a previous realization of the method is provided. A way to minimize the number of basis functions required for convergence is given. An easy way to obtain exactly unitary and symmetric $S$ matrix from calculations is pointed out. The method is tested in one- and two-channel $np$ scattering problems with the Daejeon $NN$ interaction. It is shown that excellent convergence can be reached even when only oscillator states with low number of excitation quanta are retained.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes and refines a projection-onto-localized-states method that extends the no-core shell model to continuum and clusterized bound states, improves basis convergence and S-matrix properties, and tests the approach on one- and two-channel np scattering with the Daejeon NN interaction.
AI.motivation: To provide a simple method for describing reactions and clustering and for extending the no-core shell model to continuum and clusterized bound states, while critically assessing and improving a previous realization of the method.
AI.method: The projection-onto-localized-states method is examined, a previous realization is critically analyzed, and a way to minimize the number of basis functions needed for convergence is given. An easy route to an exactly unitary and symmetric S matrix is identified. The method is tested in one- and two-channel np scattering problems using the Daejeon NN interaction and low-excitation oscillator states.
AI.result: Excellent convergence is achieved even when only oscillator states with a low number of excitation quanta are retained in the one- and two-channel np scattering tests. The method also allows an exactly unitary and symmetric S matrix to be obtained from calculations.
AI.conclusion: The method offers a simple extension of the no-core shell model to continuum and clusterized bound states and can achieve efficient convergence with low-excitation oscillator bases while providing unitary and symmetric S matrices. The abstract does not provide further applications or detailed numerical convergence data.

title: Finite temperature and pressure structural relaxations including zero-point motion and anharmonicity
summary: At finite temperature and pressure, the equilibrium structure of a crystal minimizes the Gibbs free energy rather than the static Born-Oppenheimer energy. We present WARP (Wyckoff-constrained Anharmonic Relaxations at Pressure and temperature), a symmetry-constrained, variable-cell relaxation based on the stochastic temperature-dependent effective potential method, including anharmonicity and zero-point motion. Every position update is projected onto Wyckoff positions and every strain onto symmetric strains, so a relaxation can raise the symmetry but never lower it. For aluminum, the thermal expansion follows measurements at cryogenic temperatures, including the quantum plateau below 50 K. For lanthanum hydrides at megabar pressures, equations of state agree with phonon-based and path-integral calculations, and LaH$_{10}$ relaxes from its rhombohedral static minimum to the observed cubic phase, also with a machine-learned potential fine-tuned on 150 supercells. For brucite, Mg(OD)$_2$, lattice parameters, bond distances and thermal expansion agree with neutron diffraction, and the O-D isotope effect is captured.

AI.tldr: WARP performs symmetry-constrained variable-cell crystal relaxations at finite temperature and pressure using a stochastic temperature-dependent effective potential that includes anharmonicity and zero-point motion, with validation on aluminum, lanthanum hydrides, and brucite.
AI.motivation: At finite temperature and pressure, a crystal's equilibrium structure minimizes the Gibbs free energy rather than the static Born-Oppenheimer energy, so relaxations must account for thermal and quantum nuclear effects while preserving crystal symmetry.
AI.method: The authors introduce WARP (Wyckoff-constrained Anharmonic Relaxations at Pressure and temperature), a symmetry-constrained variable-cell relaxation based on the stochastic temperature-dependent effective potential method, including anharmonicity and zero-point motion. Position updates are projected onto Wyckoff positions and strains onto symmetric strains, so symmetry can be raised but not lowered. Applications include aluminum, lanthanum hydrides at megabar pressures, LaH10 with a machine-learned potential fine-tuned on 150 supercells, and brucite Mg(OD)2.
AI.result: For aluminum, thermal expansion follows cryogenic measurements, including the quantum plateau below 50 K. For lanthanum hydrides at megabar pressures, equations of state agree with phonon-based and path-integral calculations, and LaH10 relaxes from its rhombohedral static minimum to the observed cubic phase. For brucite, lattice parameters, bond distances, and thermal expansion agree with neutron diffraction, and the O-D isotope effect is captured.
AI.conclusion: WARP enables finite-temperature and finite-pressure structural relaxation with anharmonic and zero-point effects under symmetry constraints, and its agreement with measurements and benchmark calculations supports its use for thermal expansion, equations of state, phase stability, and isotope effects.

title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows
summary: Numerical simulation of hypersonic vehicles is an attractive approach to investigate the complex phenomena involved in such technologies. For this, second-order finite volume methods (FVM) are the established method in computational fluid dynamics, with the cost of high dissipation in affordable meshes, thus needing refined ones or adaptive mesh refinements techniques to obtain accurate results. An alternative is to make use of high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods, in particular discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM), once it achieves higher formal order of accuracy on element-local polynomial bases. Therefore the goal of this work is to present the numerical simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet configuration to test and verify the applicability of the DGSEM approach for a complex hypersonic flow where shock-shock interactions occur. Results revealed to be in agreement with reference FVM solvers, thus verifying the code implementation.

AI.tldr: The paper tests a high-order discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM) on a two-dimensional scramjet configuration with hypersonic flow and shock-shock interactions, finding results consistent with reference finite volume solvers.
AI.motivation: Established second-order finite volume methods suffer from high numerical dissipation on affordable meshes, requiring refined or adaptively refined meshes for accurate hypersonic simulations; high-order DGSEM is proposed as an alternative because it provides a higher formal order of accuracy on element-local polynomial bases.
AI.method: The authors perform numerical simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet configuration using the discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM) and compare the results with reference finite volume method solvers for a complex hypersonic flow involving shock-shock interactions.
AI.result: The DGSEM results are reported to be in agreement with reference FVM solvers, thereby verifying the code implementation. Quantitative error levels, computational cost comparisons, and detailed flow-field results are not provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: DGSEM is shown to be applicable and verified for simulating a complex hypersonic scramjet flow with shock-shock interactions, supporting its use as a high-order alternative to finite volume methods; broader performance and efficiency conclusions are not detailed in the abstract.

title: Renewal Bias in Parallel Simulations of Absorbing Processes
summary: Asynchronous parallel simulations of stochastic processes with absorbing states can exhibit systematic sampling bias when trajectory durations depend on their eventual absorbing outcomes. Workers that continuously restart upon absorption preferentially record rapidly terminating trajectories within a fixed computational budget, distorting the observed ensemble statistics. We investigate this effect using a minimal renewal model with two absorbing states and state-dependent exponential durations. Renewal theory yields exact expressions for the expected number and composition of completed trajectories, showing that the resulting bias decreases algebraically with execution time but persists as the number of parallel workers increases at fixed budget. We compare continuous sampling with First-Trajectory Filtering, which retains only the initial trajectory attempted by each worker. Although finite execution deadlines introduce residual censoring bias, this bias decreases exponentially with the computational budget. An analytical mean-squared error calculation reveals budget-dependent crossover worker allocations beyond which First-Trajectory Filtering becomes more accurate despite collecting fewer trajectories. We also examine the limitations of statistical inference under severe censoring when the absorbing-state probabilities and characteristic durations are unknown. Finally, simulations of the Axelrod model near its nonequilibrium transition demonstrate the preferential sampling of rapidly absorbing fragmented configurations, illustrating the relevance of the renewal mechanism in a spatially interacting system. Our results show that increasing computational throughput does not necessarily improve statistical accuracy and highlight the importance of accounting for trajectory-duration heterogeneity in parallel simulations of absorbing processes.

AI.tldr: Asynchronous parallel simulations of stochastic processes with absorbing states can produce systematic sampling bias because workers that restart after absorption preferentially record rapidly terminating trajectories. Using a minimal renewal model, the paper derives exact expressions for completed-trajectory statistics, compares continuous sampling with First-Trajectory Filtering, analyzes censoring bias and mean-squared-error crossovers, examines inference under severe censoring, and demonstrates the effect in Axelrod-model simulations near a nonequilibrium transition.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the need to understand statistical accuracy in asynchronous parallel simulations when trajectory durations are heterogeneous and depend on eventual absorbing outcomes, since high computational throughput may distort observed ensemble statistics.
AI.method: The authors use a minimal renewal model with two absorbing states and state-dependent exponential durations. Renewal theory provides exact expressions for the expected number and composition of completed trajectories. They compare continuous sampling with First-Trajectory Filtering, analyze residual censoring bias under finite execution deadlines, derive an analytical mean-squared-error calculation for budget-dependent worker allocations, examine statistical inference under severe censoring when absorbing-state probabilities and characteristic durations are unknown, and simulate the Axelrod model near its nonequilibrium transition.
AI.result: The sampling bias decreases algebraically with execution time but persists as the number of parallel workers increases at fixed budget. First-Trajectory Filtering has residual censoring bias that decreases exponentially with computational budget. The mean-squared-error analysis reveals budget-dependent crossover worker allocations beyond which First-Trajectory Filtering becomes more accurate despite collecting fewer trajectories. Severe censoring limits statistical inference when absorbing-state probabilities and characteristic durations are unknown. Axelrod-model simulations show preferential sampling of rapidly absorbing fragmented configurations.
AI.conclusion: Increasing computational throughput does not necessarily improve statistical accuracy. Parallel simulations of absorbing processes should account for trajectory-duration heterogeneity to avoid biased ensemble statistics.

title: N-Layer quasi-geostrophic modons in a vertically sheared flow
summary: Modons, or dipolar vortices, are a form of propagating vortex solution consisting of two counterrotating regions of fluid and moving together under self-advection. They are common features of the upper ocean that can remain stable over long times, thereby transporting fluid over large distances. Here, we present a semi-analytical method for finding modon solutions in a vertically-sheared background flow using the multi-layer quasi-geostrophic framework. This method works for arbitrarily many fluid layers and builds on our previous studies of multi-layer modon solutions. We present three example of modons in a background flow, highlighting the effect of varying relative potential velocity between layers and the impact of depth-dependent potential vorticity gradients arising from surface deformation and velocity shear.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a semi-analytical method for constructing modon (dipolar vortex) solutions in a vertically sheared background flow using the multilayer quasi-geostrophic framework, with three illustrative examples.
AI.motivation: Modons are long-lived, self-advecting dipolar vortices in the upper ocean that can transport fluid over large distances; the work extends previous multilayer modon studies to vertically sheared background flows.
AI.method: A semi-analytical method within the multilayer quasi-geostrophic framework, applicable to arbitrarily many fluid layers, is used to find modon solutions in a vertically sheared background flow.
AI.result: Three example modons in a background flow are presented, illustrating effects of varying relative potential velocity between layers and depth-dependent potential vorticity gradients arising from surface deformation and velocity shear.
AI.conclusion: The method enables semi-analytical construction of multilayer quasi-geostrophic modons in vertically sheared flows; specific geophysical implications are not provided in the abstract.

title: Frequency-selective membrane-based metamaterial filters for low-insertion-loss harmonic crosstalk suppression in sub-harmonic THz receivers
summary: Parasitic reflections and standing waves fundamentally limit amplitude stability and phase fidelity in coherent continuous-wave (CW) terahertz (THz) systems. We report a complementary metamaterial filter pair designed for frequency-selective isolation at 300 GHz and 600 GHz in sub-harmonic heterodyne architectures. Fabricated on ultra-thin polyimide membranes, the filters provide more than 30 dB stopband isolation while maintaining insertion losses below 1 dB in the passband. System-level coherent-imaging experiments demonstrate effective suppression of spurious-reflection-induced interference effects and improved spectral baseline stability. The filters mitigate wavefront distortions resulting from such interferences and enhance reconstruction robustness. These results establish membrane-based metamaterial filters as compact frequency-selective isolation elements for sub-harmonic heterodyne THz detection and highlight their potential for phase-engineered imaging and sensing applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a pair of membrane-based complementary metamaterial filters for frequency-selective isolation at 300 GHz and 600 GHz in sub-harmonic heterodyne terahertz receivers, achieving high stopband rejection with low passband insertion loss and improved coherent-imaging stability.
AI.motivation: Parasitic reflections and standing waves fundamentally limit amplitude stability and phase fidelity in coherent continuous-wave terahertz systems, motivating compact frequency-selective isolation to suppress harmonic crosstalk and spurious-reflection interference in sub-harmonic heterodyne architectures.
AI.method: A complementary metamaterial filter pair was designed for frequency-selective isolation at 300 GHz and 600 GHz and fabricated on ultra-thin polyimide membranes. Its performance was evaluated through stopband/passband measurements and system-level coherent-imaging experiments.
AI.result: The filters provide more than 30 dB stopband isolation while maintaining passband insertion loss below 1 dB. Coherent-imaging experiments show suppression of spurious-reflection-induced interference, improved spectral baseline stability, mitigation of wavefront distortions, and enhanced reconstruction robustness.
AI.conclusion: Membrane-based metamaterial filters are established as compact frequency-selective isolation elements for sub-harmonic heterodyne terahertz detection, with potential for phase-engineered imaging and sensing applications.

title: A Hierarchy of Fast and Strong Signatures for Vertex Orbits
summary: The defining features of a physical system are its symmetries and its invariants. For a network, the symmetries are the automorphisms, and the invariants are the vertex orbits they define. Two vertices of a graph may appear structurally indistinguishable without being interchangeable under any graph automorphism. Distinguishing apparent similarity from genuine symmetry lies at the heart of the vertex-orbit partition problem. In this work, we develop a hierarchy of increasingly expressive, automorphism-invariant signatures that draw on the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian and the Dirac operator to reveal subtle structural differences. Guided by a sequence of counterexamples, we progressively strengthen these signatures, ultimately incorporating probing techniques, which are temporary structural perturbations, that expose the hidden distinctions in the original unperturbed graph. We evaluate our approach across diverse benchmark families, recovering exact orbit partitions in challenging instances, including graphs that resist low-dimensional Weisfeiler--Leman refinement. We also examine the computational and numerical limitations of our constructions, distinguishing empirical success from theoretical completeness. Our findings highlight the potential of spectral and probing-based methods for uncovering the structural distinctions that define vertex orbit.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a hierarchy of automorphism-invariant spectral signatures, based on the graph Laplacian and Dirac operator and strengthened by probing perturbations, to distinguish vertex orbits and recover exact orbit partitions on challenging graph benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Vertex orbits are key invariants of graph symmetry, but structurally similar vertices may not be interchangeable under any automorphism. The work aims to separate apparent similarity from genuine symmetry and to address the vertex-orbit partition problem, including cases that resist low-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman refinement.
AI.method: The authors construct increasingly expressive automorphism-invariant signatures using spectral properties of the graph Laplacian and the Dirac operator. Guided by counterexamples, they progressively strengthen the hierarchy and incorporate probing techniques, which are temporary structural perturbations intended to expose distinctions hidden in the original unperturbed graph. They evaluate the approach on diverse benchmark families and analyze computational and numerical limitations.
AI.result: The approach recovers exact orbit partitions in challenging instances, including graphs that resist low-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman refinement. The paper also identifies computational and numerical limitations of the constructions and distinguishes empirical success from theoretical completeness.
AI.conclusion: Spectral and probing-based methods show potential for uncovering structural distinctions that define vertex orbits, though their success is empirically demonstrated rather than established as theoretically complete.

title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
summary: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.

title: Non-Equilibrium Ising-Bloch Transition in Polarization Cavity Solitons

summary: Polarization cavity solitons in coherently driven Kerr resonators undergo a sequence of dynamical bifurcations as the cavity detuning is increased. title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
summary: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.

title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality
summary: Variational principles for dissipative processes come in two families: minimum principles at nonequilibrium stationary states (Helmholtz, Kirchhoff, Prigogine) and maximum principles for relaxation in continuum mechanics (Ziegler, Hackl, Fischer). We contribute to the understanding of the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) by investigating its extremal properties, and uncover the connection between the two families, whose distinction was recently made precise for diffusion: the extremal character is decided by the regime, which is either relaxation at frozen state, as in a closed system (maximum dissipation), or a driven stationary state in an open system (minimum dissipation), while the underlying Rayleighian functional is convex and minimized in both cases. We further examine the Reynolds transport theorem, a useful tool for fixing the energy rates of continua, and the role of inertia, recently argued to lie beyond the reach of Rayleighian principles. With inertia the driving force must be held fixed during the variation, which is less elegant than in the inertialess case, where it is a state function. Writing the energy rate as rates times driving forces still yields the correct equations, and an extremal statement survives whenever the frozen force does not depend on the varied rate. This holds directly for unsteady Stokes flow, and for Navier-Stokes flow after a change to material coordinates, in which the particle acceleration is the second time derivative of the state and the convective term, nonvariational in the Eulerian description, does not appear. The framework is tested on the Navier-Stokes family (Stokes, unsteady Stokes, and Navier-Stokes flow, in order of increasing complexity) and on dissipative Lagrangian mechanics.
